messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan is a 29-year-old jeweler who spent eight months overseas as part of a civilian relief team in a war zone. What he returns to most often in telling the story is not a single clean sequence but a cluster of moments inside a field clinic after a nearby blast: children brought in screaming, one after another, the crush of bodies, someone grabbing his arm from behind before he had even turned, and the pounding in his own chest so hard he thought he might black out. He remembers trying to sort supplies with shaking hands while the room filled with crying, dust, and the metallic awareness that anything around him could become dangerous. Even now, what makes those moments feel unfinished is how quickly his body seemed to learn the scene. The sound of children crying, an unexpected touch, or the sudden sensation of his heart racing can still pull the whole experience back without warning, with a force that feels more real than ordinary remembering.

Since coming home, Ethan has gone back to work at a jewelry bench in a small retail studio, but the shop floor has become one of the places where his symptoms are most visible. When a child in the neighboring storefront starts wailing, he does not just think about the war zone; the clinic is suddenly there around him, vivid and immediate. At times he cannot even picture the original scene clearly, yet the fear arrives in full intensity anyway, as if his body has skipped ahead of his mind. If a customer touches his shoulder unexpectedly while he is setting a stone, or if he notices his pulse jump after using a torch, the memory comes over him in the same abrupt way. Because these episodes can erupt from so little, he has grown convinced that danger is hidden inside ordinary sensations and sounds.

That conviction shapes how he moves through space. In the jewelry store he automatically chooses the stool with his back to the wall and a clear view of the entrance, the display cases, and whatever hard object could be used as a weapon if something happened. He notices tools, glass edges, letter openers, heavy brass lamps, and customers’ hands before he notices their faces. Coworkers have told him the shop is safe, but he finds he cannot take that in; the idea of safety feels like something other people say, not something he can trust. In that keyed-up state, the room is full of cues that keep his body braced, and once he is scanning like this, his chest starts pounding more easily, a brush past him feels instantly charged, and the same crying child outside seems impossible to tune out. The threat feels so present that the memory sits close to the surface.

When the memory surges, Ethan tries hard to manage it rather than get pulled under. He tells himself that other people had it worse, that he got out alive, that he should be grateful and keep perspective. He also forces himself toward bright, corrective thoughts—telling himself to focus on the good, to stay positive, to stop dwelling. For a few moments this can look composed from the outside, but internally it leaves him straining against the experience. The more forcefully he pushes for positivity or compares his suffering downward, the more abrupt and alien the return of the memory feels, as though it has broken through despite his efforts. He has started to dread not only the memories themselves but the sense that they can overtake him even while he is trying to master them.

Over months, these strategies have spread into habits that keep the problem going. He scans every room for exits and possible weapons before he can relax enough to speak naturally. In restaurants he asks for the corner seat facing the door; in the workshop he positions trays and tools so no one can come up behind him. This constant checking makes him feel temporarily less exposed, but it also keeps proving to him that vigilance is necessary. His body stays tense, his heart is quick to race, and once that happens he is primed for the next wave of memory. He has also become more reactive to the triggers he fears most: a child crying in the mall can ruin the rest of his day, and an unexpected touch from a colleague now makes him jerk so sharply that he has begun avoiding shared tasks at the bench.

Ethan finally sought help after startling violently when an apprentice tapped him from behind while a customer’s toddler cried near the counter. He dropped a piece he had been setting and later could not shake the feeling that he had been back in the field clinic, even though he knew where he was. What frightened him most was that ordinary life now seemed organized around anticipating the next jolt—watching, bracing, correcting his thoughts, and still not being safe from the memory. He says he wants to keep working with his hands and be able to believe, even briefly, that a room in his own city is just a room.
